rules.name: Project below model threshold
rules.short_description: A small project sits beside other projects and may duplicate configuration and release work.
rules.long_description:
A small project can require as much connection, package, and release configuration as a larger one. Review whether that separation serves a clear ownership or release need. Separate projects do not inherently lose lineage: dbt supports project-qualified ref() calls when cross-project dependencies are configured.

This rule reports projects at or below micro_project_threshold (default 5 models), only when the portfolio contains at least two projects. The threshold is a local consolidation policy, not a dbt limit.

## References

- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
- [dbt_project.yml](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt_project.yml)
rules.remediation: Consider moving the models into a sibling project if they share ownership and a release schedule. Use ref() for model dependencies. Keep separate projects when the boundary is useful; configure supported cross-project dependencies where appropriate and check support in the deployed runtime.

examples.title: Project below model threshold
examples.bad: # portfolio: project `orders_load` has 1 model next to 3 sibling projects
examples.good: # one project `warehouse` holds all models; ref() links them

rules.name: Sibling projects share source tables
rules.short_description: Two or more projects read the same logical source and table names; review their physical locations and ownership.
rules.long_description:
A source() call records a dependency on a declared source. Two projects that use the same logical source and table names do not necessarily use the same physical table. Shared input alone also does not create a dependency between their models.

This rule finds matching source() name pairs across projects. Check database, schema, identifier, and quoting before deciding that definitions are duplicates.

## References

- [About source function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/source)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
- [identifier](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/identifier)
rules.remediation: Compare the source definitions and actual target locations. Consolidate shared definitions if the projects will be merged. If they stay separate, document the common source and its owner. Use a supported cross-project ref when a model actually depends on another project's model; do not invent an ordering dependency between independent readers.

examples.title: Sibling projects share source tables
examples.bad:
# project a: select * from {{ source('raw','orders') }}
# project b: select * from {{ source('raw','orders') }}
examples.good: # one project defines source raw.orders once; models use ref()

rules.name: Project configuration repeated across siblings
rules.short_description: Three or more projects maintain separate configuration and packages; declared package versions may differ.
rules.long_description:
Each project maintains its own configuration and package declarations. Similar projects can drift when only some receive an update. This rule prompts a review for portfolios with at least three projects and reports differing package versions. The project-count threshold is local policy; it does not prove that the configuration is identical or that differing versions are wrong.

## References

- [Packages](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/packages)
- [dbt_project.yml](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt_project.yml)
rules.remediation: Consolidate projects when a common configuration and release schedule fit their ownership. Otherwise, agree on compatible package versions and review upgrades across the affected projects. Run dbt deps after changing package declarations and retain the resulting package-lock.yml for reproducible installs.

examples.title: Project config duplicated across siblings
examples.good: # one packages.yml pins dbt_utils 1.3.0 for all models

rules.name: profiles.yml is inside the project directory
rules.short_description: A profiles.yml file in the project can expose connection details if it enters version control.
rules.long_description:
profiles.yml configures connections and can contain credentials. A file at the project root is not itself proof of a leaked secret, but it can be committed with the project. OPS0002 checks for literal credentials separately.

This rule reports information when Git ignores the file. It reports a warning when the file is tracked, untracked, or its Git status is unknown.

## References

- [About profiles.yml](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/local/profiles.yml)
- [Git - gitignore Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore)
rules.remediation: Prefer ~/.dbt/profiles.yml or a profiles directory supported by the installed dbt runtime. Keep only a redacted profiles.yml.sample in the repository. Add the real file to .gitignore. If Git already tracks it, remove it from the index after review; adding an ignore pattern does not untrack it. Handle any exposed credentials through your incident process.

examples.title: profiles.yml present in the project directory
examples.good:
my_project/
  dbt_project.yml
  profiles.yml.sample   # redacted; real file in ~/.dbt/

rules.name: Converter placeholders remain in project configuration
rules.short_description: Project configuration contains converter placeholders such as YOUR_PROJECT_NAME or YOUR_DB.
rules.long_description:
Converter placeholders are values to replace before deployment. A placeholder in a project, profile, database, or schema setting can select a nonexistent or unintended resource. This rule finds known placeholder text; it does not verify the intended replacement.

## References

- [dbt_project.yml](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt_project.yml)
- [About target variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/target)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Get the real project, profile, database, and schema names from the owner or original connection. For relation locations, follow the local PRJ0009 policy: keep schema and identifiers literal; use a literal database or explicit target.name branches with an invalid_database fallback. Keep variable declarations needed by other value reads. Check the target already selected by orchestration; do not change its invocation as part of this fix.

examples.title: Converter placeholders in project config
examples.good:
name: sales_dw
profile: sales_dw

rules.name: dbt projects chained through Snowflake tasks
rules.short_description: Orchestration SQL has at least two EXECUTE DBT PROJECT calls; review where dependency ordering belongs.
rules.long_description:
Snowflake task graphs can order dbt project executions. That ordering is separate from the model dependencies dbt records through ref(). This rule finds at least two EXECUTE DBT PROJECT calls in orchestration SQL; the count alone does not prove a broken dependency. Consolidation is a local architecture recommendation, not a restriction on task graphs.

## References

- [Create a sequence of tasks with a task graph](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tasks-graphs)
- [About dbt build command](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/commands/build)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
rules.remediation: If the projects form one pipeline with shared ownership, consider merging them and expressing model dependencies with ref(). A dbt build then runs selected resources in dependency order; independent branches can still run concurrently. Keep tasks for the required schedule and external dependencies. If projects remain separate, retain and document their ordering contract.

references.title: Create a sequence of tasks with a task graph

examples.title: dbt projects chained via Snowflake Tasks
examples.good: -- one project; one task runs `dbt build` over the whole graph

rules.name: Baseline packages are not declared
rules.short_description: The project does not declare dbt_constraints or dbt_semantic_view in packages.yml.
rules.long_description:
This estate expects dbt_constraints and dbt_semantic_view in packages.yml. This is local policy, not a requirement for all dbt projects. dbt_constraints can create constraint metadata from tests on supported table models. Standard Snowflake tables do not enforce PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, or UNIQUE constraints. dbt_semantic_view supplies a semantic_view materialization; installing it does not convert ordinary models automatically.

## References

- [Packages](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/packages)
- [Overview of constraints](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/constraints-overview)
- [dbt Constraints package](https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/dbt_constraints)
- [Snowflake Semantic View dbt Package](https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/dbt_semantic_view)
rules.remediation: Check which missing packages the project needs, select compatible versions, add them to packages.yml, and run dbt deps. Validate package support in the deployed runtime. Run key tests regularly when using dbt_constraints, especially with RELY constraints. Add explicit semantic-view model definitions when using dbt_semantic_view. Document an exception if the baseline package policy does not apply.

examples.title: Required baseline packages not declared
examples.good:
# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.3.0
  - package: Snowflake-Labs/dbt_constraints
    version: [">=1.0.0", "<2.0.0"]
  - package: Snowflake-Labs/dbt_semantic_view
    version: [">=1.0.0", "<2.0.0"]

rules.name: Generated directories are not ignored by Git
rules.short_description: target/, logs/, or dbt_packages/ exists without a matching .gitignore entry.
rules.long_description:
Generated build output, logs, and installed packages usually do not belong in source control. A committed manifest can also become stale. This rule checks the project's generated directories and .gitignore entries; retain an artifact deliberately only with a documented reason. Do not treat package-lock.yml as an installed-package directory.

## References

- [Git - gitignore Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore)
- [Packages](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/packages)
rules.remediation: Add ignore patterns for the generated target/, logs/, and dbt_packages/ directories. Review tracked files before using git rm -r --cached on the specific generated paths. That command removes them from the index while keeping local files. Keep package declarations and the dependency lockfile under version control.

examples.title: Build artifact directories not in .gitignore
examples.good:
# .gitignore
target/
logs/
dbt_packages/

rules.name: Relation location uses a variable
rules.short_description: A source or model database, schema, identifier, or alias uses var() or env_var().
rules.long_description:
This rule finds variable calls in source locations, model config() locations, and folder-level +database, +schema, or +alias settings. A manifest describes the values used for one compilation. Identical Jinja text in two projects does not prove that both resolve to the same relation.

The local consolidation policy prefers explicit locations. dbt permits variables; their use is not inherently invalid. Model config() sites are grouped by project in context.files. YAML sites are reported separately.

## References

- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
- [About target variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/target)
- [Defining a database source property](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/database)
- [Defining a schema source property](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/schema)
- [identifier](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/identifier)
rules.remediation: Remove variable uses from the affected location settings. Keep schema and identifiers literal. For one environment, use a literal database. For multiple environments, map the existing target names to real databases and use invalid_database as the fallback. Confirm values with the owner; do not invent empty defaults. Keep each declaration that still supplies a non-location value. Existing --vars keys stop affecting only the removed location uses. Verify the current orchestration target without changing its invocation.

examples.title: Var-driven source schema
examples.good:
sources:
  - name: raw
    schema: RAW_INPUT

rules.name: Code branches on target.name
rules.short_description: A model, macro, YAML value, or hook compares target.name and can render differently for each target.
rules.long_description:
This rule finds target.name in conditional expressions and comparisons. The active target controls which branch renders, so a manifest from one target does not describe every branch. dbt supports target-specific logic. This finding asks for a review, not the removal of every condition. Do not assume that orchestration selects prod without checking its actual target.

## References

- [About target variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/target)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
rules.remediation: Check the target selected by each caller and verify every supported branch. Keep model dependencies consistent across targets. Use profile attributes for ordinary connection settings where appropriate. Retain an explicit database mapping required by the local PRJ0009/PRJ0021 policy; this rule does not require replacing it with a location variable. Document intentional target-specific limits or sampling.

examples.title: Target branch in source
examples.good: database: "{{ target.database }}"

rules.name: Project configuration reads env_var()
rules.short_description: A project, model, or source configuration uses an environment variable and can change between processes.
rules.long_description:
dbt permits env_var() in supported Jinja contexts. When a variable controls a relation name or dependency, different process environments can produce different compiled projects. This rule scans project configuration, model config() arguments, and source or model YAML. It excludes profiles.yml. Support for a particular variable in native EXECUTE DBT PROJECT must be checked in that runtime.

## References

- [About env_var function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/env_var)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Identify each variable's purpose and document who supplies it. Use explicit relation locations under the local PRJ0009 policy. For other non-secret values, choose a literal or documented dbt variable when that makes the contract clearer. Keep secrets in a supported credential channel; never replace them with committed literals. Document intentional environment-dependent behavior.

examples.title: env_var in folder config
examples.good: +database: "{{ target.database }}"

rules.name: Variable defaults differ across projects
rules.short_description: Two or more projects declare the same variable name with different default values.
rules.long_description:
A merge can change which default supplies a variable. dbt supports global and package-scoped variables, and command-line variables take precedence. This rule reports each name with differing declarations across projects. Its scalar comparison treats 100 and "100" as equal; that is a detector convention, not a claim that every dbt use treats them alike.

## References

- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Identify the meaning of each declaration before merging. Agree on one default when the meanings match. Otherwise rename the variables by purpose or retain valid package scopes. Scope names must match resources that remain separate packages; a former project name does not preserve scope automatically after its models move into one project.

examples.title: Different defaults
examples.bad:
# a/dbt_project.yml
vars:
  InputSchema: TD_PARAM_SCHEMA
# b/dbt_project.yml
vars:
  InputSchema: ORA_PARAM_SCHEMA
examples.good:
# one scoped value per project
vars:
  a:
    InputSchema: TD_PARAM_SCHEMA

rules.name: Variable default repeats its name
rules.short_description: A var() call uses its own key as its fallback value, such as var('pRegion', 'pRegion').
rules.long_description:
When a variable is not supplied, var() can return its call-site default. A default that repeats the key often preserves converter placeholder text. A filter may then match no rows, although the exact result depends on the data. This rule excludes reads inside hook strings. Keep the default only if the literal key text is the intended value.

## References

- [About var function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/var)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: For value reads, choose a real default or remove the fallback so a missing variable raises a compilation error. For relation locations, get the real values from the owner and follow PRJ0009/PRJ0021 instead. Review every read separately; a valid fallback at one site does not make a different site safe.

examples.title: Sentinel default
examples.good: WHERE Region = '{{ var('pRegion') }}'  -- vars: pRegion: EMEA

rules.name: A used variable has an empty default
rules.short_description: A declared variable is empty or null, and a model, macro, or YAML file reads it.
rules.long_description:
An empty or null default can leave required conversion input unspecified. Its effect depends on each read: a filter may match no rows, or rendered SQL may fail. An SSC-FDM-DS0006 marker indicates that the converter left a value for review; it does not supply the value.

This rule groups affected variables by project at the vars: block. context.vars lists them, and context.reads lists their uses. An empty value can be valid when the contract explicitly allows it.

## References

- [About var function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/var)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Check every listed value read. Set the intended default in dbt_project.yml, or document the caller that supplies --vars on every run. Follow PRJ0009/PRJ0021 for location reads rather than filling in a location variable. Remove an SSC-FDM-DS0006 marker only after resolving the missing input and validating its uses.

examples.title: Empty required var
examples.good:
vars:
  pRunDate: '2024-01-01'

rules.name: Informatica session variable has a placeholder
rules.short_description: A used Informatica session variable has a null, empty, or 1753-01-01 placeholder.
rules.long_description:
This migration rule finds known session-variable names with placeholder values. Examples include SESSSTARTTIME, WORKFLOWSTARTTIME, PMSESSIONNAME, and PMWORKFLOWNAME. A caller may supply real values through --vars; the placeholder alone does not prove that it does. Keep a caller-supplied name until its contract has been checked.

PRJ0017 owns variables with no detected reads. This rule covers used session variables, so the two findings do not ask for opposite edits to one declaration.

## References

- [About run_started_at variable](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/run_started_at)
- [About invocation_id](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/invocation_id)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: For each time read, decide whether it means the dbt invocation start or the original workflow/session time. Use run_started_at only for the former, with the required formatting and timezone; otherwise keep the caller-supplied value. Use invocation_id only for a dbt command UUID, not as a replacement for a workflow or session name. Use a confirmed literal for stable names. Remove a placeholder declaration only after replacing all its reads, and retain it if orchestration still supplies it.

examples.title: Placeholder session var
examples.good:
# value supplied per run
# dbt build --vars '{SESSSTARTTIME: "2024-05-01 00:00:00"}'

rules.name: Variable read has no declared value or default
rules.short_description: A required var() read has no detected declaration, call-site default, or recognized guard.
rules.long_description:
dbt raises a compilation error when a required variable has no value. This rule checks each read against detected project declarations, including the current project's scope. A call-site default covers only that read. Sentinel defaults belong to PRJ0013. Relation-location reads belong to PRJ0021/PRJ0022.

Before acting, check inputs outside this scan, such as a parent project or --vars. Newer dbt versions can also supply variables through vars.yml. Absence from this scan is not proof that the runtime has no value.

## References

- [About var function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/var)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: For each reported value read, add a safe declared value or an intentional call-site default. If the caller supplies the variable, document that contract in the waiver. Do not add a location default merely to silence this check; use the relation rule for location reads. Confirm that any guard protects this read, not just another use of the same variable.

examples.title: Undeclared var
examples.bad: select * from t where d = '{{ var('run_date') }}'
examples.good:
# dbt_project.yml
vars:
  run_date: '2024-01-01'

rules.name: Declared variable has no detected reads
rules.short_description: A variable in dbt_project.yml has no detected literal-key reads in models, macros, YAML, or hooks.
rules.long_description:
Unused declarations make the input contract harder to review. This rule skips package-scoped declarations and skips the check when a dynamic var() key prevents a complete read list. Passing a key through --vars does not itself consume the value.

Findings are grouped at the project vars: block. context.vars lists unread variables. context.session_vars identifies converter-emitted session variables that the local migration policy allows you to keep.

## References

- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
- [About var function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/var)
rules.remediation: Check package and dynamic uses before deleting a declaration. Keep context.session_vars under the migration policy. Before deleting an unread watermark variable, review Load patterns & incremental findings: a missing read may indicate a lost incremental filter. Remove other unused keys from dbt_project.yml. An orchestration caller can keep passing a now-unused key, but document any deliberate exception.

examples.title: Unused var
examples.good: vars: {}

rules.name: Variable declarations disagree within a project
rules.short_description: A variable key appears more than once with different values, either globally or in a scoped block.
rules.long_description:
This rule finds differing global and scoped declarations, and repeated YAML keys under vars:. dbt has defined precedence for global, package-scoped, and command-line variables. An intentional package override is valid; duplicate keys in the same mapping are not a clear way to express that contract.

## References

- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Keep one declaration per scope. If scoped overrides are intentional, document which resources receive each value and confirm the package names. Otherwise choose one default or rename variables with different meanings. Check command-line overrides before deciding which value a run receives.

examples.title: Duplicate declaration
examples.bad:
vars:
  region: EMEA
  demo:
    region: APAC
examples.good:
vars:
  region: EMEA

rules.name: Duplicate source declaration
rules.short_description: Source entries repeat a logical name or describe the same physical relation; verify locations before merging.
rules.long_description:
This rule groups repeated source names, repeated logical source/table pairs, and differently named tables with matching physical locations. A repeated name across projects can collide after consolidation. Exact duplicate-source diagnostics differ by dbt engine and version; do not rely on a parser keeping one definition.

Compare database, schema, identifier, and quoting. dbt defaults a source's schema to its source name, its identifier to the table name, and its database to the target database. Equal logical names, equal Jinja text, or equal source-block locations alone do not prove that tables are the same. Quoted Snowflake identifiers preserve case; unquoted identifiers resolve in uppercase.

Use the finding's classification:

- Consolidate verified copies of one physical relation. Keep the indicated source entry and move distinct tables into it. Preserve each identifier and all table properties. If source-level quoting differs, add explicit table quoting before moving the table so its physical identity stays unchanged.
- Rename entries for different locations under the local one-block-per-database.schema policy. Use the schema name in lower case, or database_schema when needed. Preserve distinct physical tables under collision-free logical names. Map each source() call to its own project's declaration.
- Resolve uncertain locations before editing. Identical generated placeholders describe intent, not physical proof. Confirm real target values and rerun the comparison. Ask the owner about ambiguous callers.

Do not discard a table because its name resembles a model. Remove a model-owned source only after proving the full physical identity and resolving its readers through PRJ0021 or PRJ0022. Findings list each entry as a root-relative path:line. Naming and consolidation preferences are local policy.

## References

- [About source function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/source)
- [Defining a database source property](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/database)
- [Defining a schema source property](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/schema)
- [identifier](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/identifier)
- [Configuring quoting in sources](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/quoting)
- [Identifier requirements](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/identifiers-syntax)
rules.remediation: Follow the per-entry and per-read advice. Change only the listed source() calls whose ownership is known. Keep unresolved or physically distinct tables, even when their logical names match. Preserve identifiers and quoting when moving tables. Use a literal schema and a literal database, or explicit target.name database branches with an invalid_database fallback. Keep variable declarations needed by remaining value reads. Existing orchestration variables stop affecting only the removed location uses; verify the selected target without changing orchestration.

examples.title: Same source name in two projects
examples.bad:
# a/models/sources.yml
sources:
  - name: raw
    tables: [{name: orders}]
# b/models/sources.yml
sources:
  - name: raw
    tables: [{name: orders}]
examples.good:
# merged/models/sources.yml
sources:
  - name: raw
    tables: [{name: orders}]

rules.name: Duplicate model name or relation
rules.short_description: Models share a name or resolve to one relation; confirm ownership before consolidating, merging, or renaming.
rules.long_description:
This rule groups models with the same name or the same resolved relation. A name collision inside one project prevents dbt from loading those models and is reported as an error. A collision across projects becomes relevant when they are merged. dbt also rejects two resources with one database representation within a project. Separate projects can still replace each other's table if both write the same physical relation.

Compare full database, schema, alias, and quoting semantics. The filename alone is not the relation identity. A custom alias can keep two writers on the same table after a file rename. Generated placeholders and unresolved locations need confirmation before a destructive edit.

The finding proposes one of three actions:

- Consolidate copies with SQL equal apart from comments and whitespace. Review effective configuration, hooks, and original ownership too; SQL similarity does not prove identical behavior.
- Merge different SQL that writes one fixed relation. Preserve every writer's logic and confirm the original load order, update strategy, and truncate settings.
- Rename models whose relation follows their filename. Suggested names use an m_* folder or project prefix and avoid existing model names. Caller mapping uses the m_* folder or tag; ambiguous ref() calls require owner confirmation.

Each finding lists group members as root-relative path:line values and identifies calls to change. A merge is a proposal, not proof that UNION ALL preserves the original workflow.

## References

- [Custom aliases](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/custom-aliases)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
- [Identifier requirements](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/identifiers-syntax)
rules.remediation: Verify the full physical relations and each caller's intended producer. Keep one verified duplicate and redirect its listed ref() calls before deleting the others. Merge multiple writers only after preserving their load semantics. Rename other collisions with the proposed free names, but check aliases and generated naming macros too. Do not redirect an ambiguous call or delete a writer until ownership is resolved.

examples.title: Same model name in two projects
examples.good:
a/models/stg_orders.sql
b/models/b__stg_orders.sql  -- and ref('b__stg_orders') in project b

examples.title: Two models write one table
examples.bad:
models/m_A/out.sql: {{ config(alias='HIER') }} select ...
models/m_B/out2.sql: {{ config(alias='HIER') }} select ...
examples.good: models/hier.sql: {{ config(alias='HIER') }} select ... union all select ...

rules.name: Relation reads bypass dbt dependencies
rules.short_description: Variable-built reads need location-aware ref() or source() advice; each read must use its own verified producer.
rules.long_description:
This rule groups relation reads by consumer project and table. It distinguishes same-project, cross-project, multiple-writer, external, stage, and unresolved reads. It also covers source() reads of model-owned relations. Matching uses the physical database, schema, identifier, aliases, and quoting; a table name alone does not identify a producer.

The group can contain reads with different locations or owners. Follow the advice for each read, rather than applying one replacement to the whole group. Unresolved values, identical generated placeholders, and converter self-read annotations need real location evidence from the owner or compiled target.

PRJ0022 owns cycle read sites, including cycles formed by proposed cross-project relation edges. SQL0006 owns ordinary literal model reads. Resolve PRJ0020 multiple-writer findings before choosing a producer. The local consolidation policy uses sources while projects stay separate, then acyclic refs after merging; supported dbt cross-project dependencies are another deployment-specific option.

## References

- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
- [About source function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/source)
- [Custom aliases](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/custom-aliases)
- [Configuring quoting in sources](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/quoting)
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
rules.remediation: Resolve every listed read separately. Use ref() for the verified same-project producer only when the dependency stays acyclic. After a merge, apply the same check to cross-project reads. While projects remain separate, use the specified source contract unless supported cross-project dependencies are configured. External and stage reads need their own source setup; preserve stage path suffixes and verify the required package/runtime support. Keep schema literal and use a literal database or target.name mapping with invalid_database fallback. Preserve aliases and quoting. Remove variables from the replaced location reads, but retain declarations and caller inputs for remaining value reads; PRJ0016 still owns those. Check the current orchestration target without changing its invocation.

examples.title: Hard-coded read of another project's output
examples.good:
-- merged project
select * from {{ ref('orders_out') }}

rules.name: Prior-state read closes a producer dependency cycle
rules.short_description: A read of the current or downstream producer requires a prior-state design that avoids a dependency cycle.
rules.long_description:
This rule finds variable-built, literal, source(), and unguarded this reads that refer to the current model or a downstream producer. It checks producer locations and a ref graph that includes proposed relation-read edges, including cycles after projects merge. Matching must preserve aliases and identifier quoting. Generated self-read annotations and identical placeholders describe intent; they do not prove the real physical location.

A this read is excluded only when the model is incremental and that read is guarded by is_incremental(). A safe read elsewhere in the file does not protect an unguarded read. dbt requires valid SQL when is_incremental() is true and when it is false. First builds and full refreshes must not depend on the target's prior contents.

The finding supplies read-specific dependency evidence. Do not add a ref() edge that closes the cycle, or disguise an own-table read as an external source. Resolve uncertain locations and multiple writers before relocating logic.

## References

- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
- [about this](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/this)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
- [Configuring quoting in sources](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-properties/quoting)
rules.remediation: For each listed read, move the read and all SQL that depends on it downstream into the producer as a CTE. Read this there only inside the is_incremental() branch. Give the first-build/full-refresh branch no prior state: use an empty CTE with the same typed columns, or omit the join. Remove the staging self-read and obsolete own-table source entry after resolving its readers. Use incremental materialization when the model needs prior state. Choose unique_key and incremental_strategy from the original update and load contract: upserts and prior-state full overwrites are different operations. Verify the installed adapter's overwrite behavior before selecting it. While projects stay separate, retain the documented source contract for the other project's output; apply the relocation when merging. Remove only obsolete location-variable uses and keep remaining value reads and their declarations. Recheck all physical locations, branches, and reads without changing orchestration.

examples.title: Guard prior state in the downstream producer
examples.bad: -- stage reads the table written by its downstream mart
examples.good: {% if is_incremental() %} select id from {{ this }} {% else %} select cast(null as number) as id where false {% endif %}
